Surah al-Infitar (The Cleaving) is Meccan, and its verses number nineteen.

﴿When the sky is cleaved asunder﴾ — i.e., split open for the descent of the angels, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And the day the sky shall split open with clouds and the angels will be sent down, descending﴾, and His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And the sky will be opened, and it will become gateways﴾. And the discussion regarding the raising (irtifa') of the sky is as it passed regarding the raising of the sun.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 82, verse 2:**

﴿And when the stars are scattered﴾. That is: they fall down, dispersed.

"And when the seas are burst forth" — its parts are opened into one another, so the sweet water mixes with the salt water, the barrier of separation between them disappears, and the seas become one single sea. It is also narrated that after the seas have filled, the earth drinks up the water and it becomes level; this is the meaning of "tasjir" (being set ablaze/kindled) according to al-Hasan (may Allah be pleased with him). It is also said: the waters of the seas now are stagnant and gathered, and when they are burst forth they scatter and depart. The word has also been read as "fujirat" with light stress, in the passive voice, and also in the active voice, meaning "they transgressed" (baghat), from fujur (wickedness), in view of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They do not transgress (la yabghiyan)﴾.

And when the graves are overturned (bu'thirat).

That is, their dust is turned over and their dead are brought out. Its counterpart is "bahthara," both in wording and meaning. Both are compounded from "al-ba'th" (raising/stirring up) and "al-bahth" (searching), with a "ra'" added to them.

The words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿A soul will know what it has sent forward and what it has left behind﴾ are the response (jawab) to "idha" (إذا, "when"). However, this does not mean that it knows this at the resurrection (al-ba'th). Rather, it knows it at the unfolding of the scrolls (nashr al-suhuf), as you have understood, since what is meant by these is a single time whose beginning is the first blast of the trumpet (al-nafkha al-ula) and whose end is the judgment (al-fasl) between creatures, not multiple times according to the multiplicity of the word "idha." The word is repeated only to magnify the calamities contained within its scope, and the discussion of it is like what has already passed in detail regarding its counterpart.

The meaning of "what it has sent forward and left behind" is: what it has sent ahead of good or evil deeds, and what it has left behind of good or evil practices (sunnah) that are followed after it. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Mas'ud. It is also reported from Ibn 'Abbas that it is what it sent forward of disobedience and left behind of obedience, and this is the view of Qatadah. It has also been said: what it sent forward of its wealth for itself, and what it left behind for its heirs. It has been said: what it sent forward of an obligation and left behind of an obligation. It has been said: the first of its deeds and the last of them. The meaning of its knowing in detail is as has been mentioned repeatedly before.

(p-121) ﴿O mankind, what has deceived you concerning your Lord, the Generous?﴾ That is: what thing deceived you and emboldened you to disobey Him, when you know what lies before you of complete calamities and overwhelming obstacles, and what will happen then of witnessing all your deeds? And the mention of the attribute of His generosity, exalted is He, serves to indicate that it is not something suitable to be a basis for being deceived, such that Satan misleads him and says to him: "Do whatever you wish, for your Lord is generous; He has bestowed favor upon you in this world and will do the same in the Hereafter." For that is a barren analogy and a vain wish. Rather, it is among the things that necessitate exceeding effort in turning to faith and obedience, and in refraining from disbelief and disobedience, as if it were said: "What has moved you to disobey your Lord, who is described with the attributes that deter from that and call to its opposite?"

This is the second attribute, which confirms lordship and shows His generosity, and it alerts that whoever was able to create you at the beginning is able to do so again. "Taswiyah" means making the limbs sound and well-formed, prepared for their benefits. "'Adalaka" means He balanced some of them against others so that they came into proportion and did not differ, or He turned them away from a form unsuited to them. It is also read "fa-'addalaka" with the shadda, meaning He made you well-proportioned, with harmonious creation and no disparity in it.

In what form He willed He composed you.

That is: He composed you in whatever form He willed among the various forms. The "mā" is superfluous (mazīdah), and "shā'a" (willed) is a qualifier of "ṣūrah" (form). That is: He composed you in whatever form He willed and chose for you from among the wondrous and beautiful forms, like His saying, ﴿Indeed, We created man in the best of stature﴾. And the sentence was not conjoined to what precedes it because it is an explanation (bayān) of "ʿadalaka" (He proportioned you).

"Nay" (kalla): a rebuke against being deceived by the generosity of God Most High and turning it into a pretext for disbelief and sin, although it should lead to gratitude and obedience. His saying, Most High: ﴿Nay, but you deny the Recompense﴾ is a turning away (idrab) from an implied sentence to which the discourse leads, as if it were said after the rebuke, by way of interjection: "And you do not refrain from that; rather you dare to do something greater than that, in that you deny the requital and the Resurrection altogether, or the religion of Islam, of which these two are part of its rulings; so you believe neither in questioning nor in answer, nor in reward nor in punishment." It has been said: it is as if it were said, "Indeed you do not keep to what My blessings upon you and My guidance to you necessitate, but you deny..." etc. Al-Qaffal said: "The matter is not as you say, that there is no resurrection and no rising again." Then it was said: "You are not made clear by this explanation, but you deny the Day of Recompense."

And His saying, ﴿And indeed, over you are guardians﴾, is a circumstantial clause (hal) referring to the subject of "you deny" (tukadhdhibun), indicating the invalidity of their denial and the certainty of what they deny. That is: you deny the recompense, while in fact there are over you, from Our side, guardians recording your deeds.

Translation:

﴿They know what you do﴾ of deeds, small and great, and they record it precisely, down to the speck (naqir) and the thin membrane (qitmir), so that you may be recompensed for it. And in the exalting of the two scribes by praising them is a magnification of the matter of recompense, and that it is, in the sight of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, among the momentous affairs, inasmuch as these noble ones are employed in it.

Almighty God's saying: ﴿Indeed, the righteous are surely in bliss﴾ ﴿and indeed the wicked are surely in the Blazing Fire﴾ is a resumptive statement (isti'naf) brought to explain the outcome of the recording and the writing down, namely the reward and the punishment. In the indefinite form of "bliss" (na'im) and "the Blazing Fire" (jahim) there is a magnification and a dreadful emphasis that is not hidden.

In the indefinite form of "bliss" (na'im) and "the Blazing Fire" (jahim) there is a magnification and a dreadful emphasis that is not hidden.

And His saying, ﴿they will burn in it﴾ is either an attributive description of "Hellfire" (jahim), or a resumptive clause (isti'naf) built upon a question arising from its terrifying nature, as if it were said: "What is their condition therein?" So it is answered: "They will suffer its heat."

﴿on the Day of Judgment﴾, the Day of Recompense (yawm al-jaza') which they used to deny.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 82, verse 16:

﴿And they will never be absent from it﴾ for a moment. The intended meaning is the continuity of the negation of absence, not the negation of the continuity of absence. This is because, as has been mentioned many times, a negated nominal sentence may be intended to express the continuation of the negation, not the negation of continuation, in terms of what it conveys of permanence and stability after the negation, not before it. It has also been said that its meaning is: they were not absent from it before that at all, but rather they used to find its scorching heat in their graves, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The grave is either a garden from the gardens of Paradise or a pit from the pits of the Fire."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 82, verses 17–18:

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And what will make you know what the Day of Judgment is?﴾ ﴿Then what will make you know what the Day of Judgment is?﴾ It is an exaltation of the matter of the Day of Judgment, which they deny, following an exaltation and a making-awful of its affair after an awe-inspiring description, by stating that it lies outside the sphere of creatures' comprehension in whatever form they conceive it: whatever form they imagine it in, it is above that and greater than that. That is: and what thing has made you know what the Day of Judgment is? This is on the reading where "ma" (what) in the interrogative is the predicate of "yawm al-din" (the Day of Judgment), unlike the reverse, as is the view of Sibawayh, because the locus of benefit is the predicate and not the subject, as has passed. There is no doubt that the locus of conveying awe and magnitude here is "ma" (what), that is: what strange thing is it in its awfulness and dreadfulness? As has passed more than once, the word "ma" may be used to ask for a description, although it is originally laid down for asking about the reality and explaining the name. One says: "Ma Zayd?" (What is Zayd?), and the answer is: "A writer or a physician." And the explicit mention of "yawm al-din" in the position where a pronoun would be expected is an emphasis on its awfulness and magnitude.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 82, verse 19:

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿On the Day when no soul will have power for another soul in anything, and the command that Day belongs entirely to Allah﴾ are a general explanation of the matter of the Day of Religion (Yawm al-Din) after its vagueness, and a clarification of how it lies beyond the knowledge of creatures, by way of fulfilling a promise, for the negation of their knowing it implies the gracious promise that it will be made known. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: "Every occurrence in the Qur'an of the words of Allah the Exalted ﴿What will make you know?﴾ [ma adraka] means that He has made him know it, and every occurrence in it of the words ﴿And what will make you know?﴾ [wa ma yudrika] means that it has been concealed from him."

"Yawm" is in the nominative case, being the predicate of an omitted subject, and its vowel is fatha because it is attached to an indeclinable word. It is as if it were said: It is the Day on which no soul among souls will have power for another soul among souls in anything among things... etc. Or it is in the accusative case, governed by an implied "udhkur" (remember), as if it were said, after magnifying the matter of the Day of Religion and stirring desire in him, peace be upon him, to know it: Remember the Day when no soul will have power... etc., for it will make you know what it is. It has been said that it is governed by an implied "yudanun" (they will be recompensed), but this is not the case, for it is devoid of conveying what the preceding words convey; likewise its being a substitute for "Yawm al-Din" in the nominative reading is of the same kind. Rather, the correct view in that case is the nominative, as the predicate of an omitted subject.

From the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: "Whoever recites the Surah of al-Infitar, Allah the Exalted will record for him a good deed for every drop of rain from the sky and for every grave."

And Allah the Exalted knows best.
